Mark Phillips, Founder of 11 Tribes Ventures, joins Impact Investing Roadshow to discuss his firm's founder-first venture capital thesis and their investment in NQS (National Quality Systems), a vertical AI platform transforming trauma registry management for U.S. hospital emergency departments.

Deal Highlights - NQS (National Quality Systems)
Founded by multi-time entrepreneur Mark Feinberg, NQS is a vertical AI platform designed to streamline trauma registry management for hospital emergency departments. The company addresses a highly specialized domestic market of approximately 2,400 trauma registry departments—a space previously served by a single, broad-based incumbent whose undifferentiated software left users deeply underserved.
11 Tribes co-invested alongside lead investor Long Run Capital, committing an initial $750,000 check into a priced seed round at an $8 million post-money valuation, with the total raise of $2 million split between the two firms. A defining feature of the investment was NQS's 16 signed hospital contracts at the time of closing—despite the product being six to eight weeks from launch—a rare validation of both market urgency and founder credibility.
Operating partner Carolyn Wilson, former COO of the University of Chicago Health System, provided critical domain expertise during diligence. The round closed in March 2025, the product launched within weeks, and NQS has since grown rapidly. 11 Tribes has made two additional investment tranches, including a recent $750,000 follow-on that effectively constitutes a Series A.

Through The Valley
By Mark Phillips
Every founder has a season they leave out of the story. The stretch where the company almost went under. The years of doubt, failure, and quiet identity crisis that never make it into the profile piece.
Through the Valley is a long-form interview show about those chapters. Host Mark Phillips, founder of 11 Tribes Ventures, sits down with founders and leaders to talk honestly about what it cost to get here, and who they became on the way through.

Rebuilt From Nothing & Gave His Life to Other Founders | Michael Dermer @ Lonely Entrepreneur
In October 2008, Michael Dermer had just closed a private equity round at a valuation that validated a decade of work. He had close to 900 employees and a solution wired deep into the Fortune 1000. Within a month, two of his three largest clients ceased to exist and the third needed a government bailout.
What followed was three years of twenty-hour days with no defined endpoint, no visible math, and no one to tell him when it would be over. A year earlier he had turned down an offer for the company at a number he still refuses to say out loud. Learning to stop thinking about that number was, in his words, the part of him that had to die.
Michael eventually got the company to the other side and sold it. Then a friend said one sentence in a coffee shop that redirected the rest of his life, and The Lonely Entrepreneur was born.
In this episode:
• What the first thirty days after a black swan event actually feel like from the CEO's chair
• The two rules he gave his team when the plan stopped working
• Why he insists he never felt lonely, even while building a company named for loneliness
• The letter his business partner wrote about him, read aloud for the first time
• How he now tells founders to find markets that are worth zero today
• Why he believes AI is a 2008-scale reset and what skills survive it
• What he would say to himself on the worst night in the valley

Pro Basketball to 5x Founder: A Masterclass in Resilience | Jordan Fliegel
At 28, Jordan Fliegel had a career-ending injury behind him, thirty employees in front of him, and a startup he loved so much he lived across the street from the office so he could be the first one in. Then his board told him they were replacing him as CEO, and offered him three to five million dollars at a higher valuation if he'd stay quietly and help pick his own replacement.
He said yes. Not because he agreed with it, but because saying no meant firing the people he called family. He's never talked about it publicly until now.
Jordan is the founder of CoachUp, former co-CEO of DRAFT, and now the founder and CEO of Acquisition Lab, where he helps people buy small businesses instead of starting them. In this conversation with Mark Phillips he walks through the whole valley: the demotion, the year he spent as a president whose title meant nothing, the nine months he slept in a Manhattan office while his next company was insolvent, and the day he finally came back and removed the investors who removed him.

Cancer at 30, and the Company He Built After It | Founder Brandon Aversano, The Alloy Market
In the fall of 2022 Brandon Aversano was 30 years old, away on a trip in California, and found it himself in the middle of the night. Thirty minutes after an ultrasound the chief of urology walked into the room and told him there was a 99% chance it was testicular cancer. His first thought wasn’t about himself. It was how he was going to tell his mom.
Nothing could be known before surgery. Three weeks of sitting with whether it was in one spot or everywhere. His dad had prostate cancer the year before. Brandon had built an identity on competence, distinguished scholar, Deloitte, JetBlue, JP Morgan, and the one thing he suddenly couldn’t do was be the capable one. He went on disability the day after scheduling surgery and had free time for the first time in a decade.
Mark Phillips sits with Brandon on what that season cost and what it built: the medical debt that horrified a father who hated debt, the trip to Jewelers Row with his grandmother’s jewelry where strangers offered twenty cents on the dollar, the 401k he emptied into a company, the $40,000 mobile app his co-founder told him to scrap, and the surgeon who said the book on whether it comes back is already written and he doesn’t get to read the last chapter for five years.

Why There's Shame in Getting Sober but None in the Damage | With The Maze Founder Justin Gurland
Justin Gurland arrived at rehab at eleven at night, three thousand miles from everyone he knew. He woke up the next morning in Los Angeles on Super Bowl Sunday, 2008, gave himself the finger in the mirror, and watched the Giants beat the undefeated Patriots. Then the staff turned off the game, walked everyone into a group room, and asked what each of them believed in.
He was twenty-five. He had no community, no sober person anywhere in his life to point at, and no idea what the question meant. What he said was that the Giants had just won and he could hold on to that for now. He describes the moment as meaningless on its face, a football game, a team he wasn't on. It was also the only thing he had.
Mark Phillips sits with Justin eighteen years later, five blocks from The Maze, the members club he opened in the Flatiron where hundreds of New Yorkers pay to belong to a building with no alcohol in it. They talk about the sister who told him she couldn't take it anymore, the letter his father hand-wrote for this episode, the Grateful Dead lyric he keeps returning to, and the question he still can't answer: why the shame attaches to getting sober instead of to the damage.
In this episode:
• Why he says his sister saved his life, and what happens to people who never get that conversation

Why Brutal Honesty Is the Kindest Thing an Investor Can Do, with VC Coach Charlie O’Donnell
For 20 years, Charlie O'Donnell was the most findable investor in New York. Email on the front page of his site, pitch me anything, come to the dinner. Then in May 2023 he wrote a sentence announcing his last venture deal and stopped.
The market didn't push him out. Most people in venture keep raising because it's a good job and there's always a next fund. Charlie ran Brooklyn Bridge Ventures as a solo first-check investor across more than 100 companies, and when he looked at the two available ways to keep doing it into his 40s (hire a younger version of himself, or stop looking at anything pre-revenue) he decided he'd rather not do the job at all than do it that way.
Mark Phillips sits with Charlie on what it costs to hold a career loosely: the ice cream shop that went to zero and the conversation he never had with those founders, the marathon he ran badly and blamed on the wind, the 80 days in the NICU where three term sheets got signed, and the firefighter father who played tennis in the morning and did tax returns in the afternoon and was content.

• Why Charlie stopped raising funds while the option to continue was still open
• The tradeoff he now tells every founder about before they take a check

From Losing Everything at 30 to Building the Firm That Coaches Fortune 100 Executives: Jason Jaggard
Jason Jaggard is the founder of Novus Global, one of the biggest executive coaching firms in the world whose coaches work with Global Executives, professional athletes, and Grammy-winning artists. But at 30, his life collapsed. In a single year, he quit a great job, lost 90% of his revenue, and watched his most important relationship fall apart. We talk about what broke, why it broke, and how that year became the foundation for the firm he leads today.
In this first episode of Through the Valley, Jason talks with Mark Phillips about the night he collapsed on his apartment floor, the "cold war" he entered with God, and how the tools he found in his darkest season became the foundation of a coaching firm that now serves some of the most influential leaders on Earth.
They cover why blame keeps you stuck, why self-pity is a drug, the difference between psychological safety and psychological strength, and why community is the closest thing to a bulletproof vest a founder can wear.
Through the Valley is hosted by Mark Phillips, founder of 11 Tribes Ventures, and explores the seasons of loss, failure, and doubt behind remarkable careers.

This timely ATLalts podcast episode highlights the multifaceted landscape of private credit and alternative investment solutions, with a particular emphasis on the strategic considerations necessary for optimizing portfolio allocations in an increasingly volatile market environment. Our guest, Brook Scardina, Managing Partner - Capital Markets & Investments at Oak Real Estate Partners, brings a wealth of experience from his extensive tenure in institutional investing, where he adeptly navigated the complexities of asset management for noteable foundations and endowments such as UNC Management Company, UPS Pension Plan, and Georgia Tech Foundation.
In a market characterized by recent stock market volatility, daily headlines of tariffs, uncertain fed policy, and fluctuating economic indicators, Scardina argues for the critical importance of incorporating alternative investments and private credit into investment portfolios as a means of enhancing diversification, mitigating risk, and earning attractive risk-adjusted yields, particularly in light of the diminishing returns expected from traditional equity markets. Furthermore, he articulates the structural advantages inherent in certain areas of the private credit space, such as reduced competition and the ability to capitalize on niche lending opportunities in short-duration real estate bridge lending, that larger institutions and banks overlook or can't pursue, thus providing a compelling rationale for investors to re-evaluate their asset allocation strategies. This discussion not only seeks to educate and inform but also to engage listeners in a deeper understanding of how nuanced approaches to private credit can serve as a cornerstone for achieving robust financial outcomes in a fluctuating and rapidly evolving economic landscape.
The conversation delves into the intricate dynamics of private credit as a pivotal component of alternative investment strategies, and how investors can benefit from the different areas of this rapidly growing market. He emphasizes the necessity for investors to reassess their portfolios, particularly in light of the potential for a more protracted low expected return environment from equities and fixed income, advocating for an incremental allocation to private credit as a means of enhancing risk-adjusted returns.
Scardina’s extensive background in managing large-scale investment portfolios for prestigious institutions at endowments, foundations, and corporate pension plans, equips him with the insights necessary to help educate listeners on the growing field and inherent complexities of private credit. He explores the various iterations within the private credit sector, such as subordinated debt and mezzanine financing, highlighting their distinct risk-return profiles. The episode elaborates on OREP's strategic approach to risk mitigation, underscoring the importance of customized financing solutions that align with the specific objectives of institutional investors.
Moreover, Scardina’s case studies during the episode serve as practical illustrations of how OREP effectively addresses the financing needs of borrowers within the real estate private credit space where OREP competes, particularly in sectors where traditional lenders are typically hesitant to engage. Every founder has a season they leave out of the story. The stretch where the company almost went under. The years of doubt, failure, and quiet identity crisis that never make it into the profile piece.
Through the Valley is a long-form interview show about those chapters. Host Mark Phillips, founder of 11 Tribes Ventures, sits down with founders and leaders to talk honestly about what it cost to get here, and who they became on the way through.
New episodes every Wednesday.

Rebuilt From Nothing & Gave His Life to Other Founders | Michael Dermer @ Lonely Entrepreneur
In October 2008, Michael Dermer had just closed a private equity round at a valuation that validated a decade of work. He had close to 900 employees and a solution wired deep into the Fortune 1000. Within a month, two of his three largest clients ceased to exist and the third needed a government bailout. What followed was three years of twenty-hour days with no defined endpoint, no visible math, and no one to tell him when it would be over. A year earlier he had turned down an offer for the company at a number he still refuses to say out loud. Learning to stop thinking about that number was, in his words, the part of him that had to die. Michael eventually got the company to the other side and sold it. Then a friend said one sentence in a coffee shop that redirected the rest of his life, and The Lonely Entrepreneur was born. In this episode: • What the first thirty days after a black swan event actually feel like from the CEO's chair • The two rules he gave his team when the plan stopped working • Why he insists he never felt lonely, even while building a company named for loneliness • The letter his business partner wrote about him, read aloud for the first time • How he now tells founders to find markets that are worth zero today • Why he believes AI is a 2008-scale reset and what skills survive it • What he would say to himself on the worst night in the valley Subscribe to Through the Valley wherever you listen. New episodes on YouTube, Spotify, and Apple Podcasts. Find Michael at lonelyentrepreneur.com. Pro Basketball to 5x Founder: A Masterclass in Resilience | Jordan Fliegel
At 28, Jordan Fliegel had a career-ending injury behind him, thirty employees in front of him, and a startup he loved so much he lived across the street from the office so he could be the first one in. Then his board told him they were replacing him as CEO, and offered him three to five million dollars at a higher valuation if he'd stay quietly and help pick his own replacement. He said yes. Not because he agreed with it, but because saying no meant firing the people he called family. He's never talked about it publicly until now. Jordan is the founder of CoachUp, former co-CEO of DRAFT, and now the founder and CEO of Acquisition Lab, where he helps people buy small businesses instead of starting them. In this conversation with Mark Phillips he walks through the whole valley: the demotion, the year he spent as a president whose title meant nothing, the nine months he slept in a Manhattan office while his next company was insolvent, and the day he finally came back and removed the investors who removed him. In this episode: The napkin math that shows exactly when your investors' incentives stop matching yoursWhy he ran through Boston in tears to a mentor's office with no appointmentWhat it feels like to sit in meetings where every good idea you offer undermines your own successorHow he told ten employees the money was gone, and what he had to say to the one he couldn't saveThe letter his mentor wrote him, read out loud for the first timeWhy he took a company from "we can't pay our bills" to a $48M exitThe Jocko Willink rule he now applies to every piece of bad news Subscribe for new episodes of Through the Valley every week. Cancer at 30, and the Company He Built After It | Founder Brandon Aversano, The Alloy Market
In the fall of 2022 Brandon Aversano was 30 years old, away on a trip in California, and found it himself in the middle of the night. Thirty minutes after an ultrasound the chief of urology walked into the room and told him there was a 99% chance it was testicular cancer. His first thought wasn’t about himself. It was how he was going to tell his mom. Nothing could be known before surgery. Three weeks of sitting with whether it was in one spot or everywhere. His dad had prostate cancer the year before. Brandon had built an identity on competence, distinguished scholar, Deloitte, JetBlue, JP Morgan, and the one thing he suddenly couldn’t do was be the capable one. He went on disability the day after scheduling surgery and had free time for the first time in a decade. Mark Phillips sits with Brandon on what that season cost and what it built: the medical debt that horrified a father who hated debt, the trip to Jewelers Row with his grandmother’s jewelry where strangers offered twenty cents on the dollar, the 401k he emptied into a company, the $40,000 mobile app his co-founder told him to scrap, and the surgeon who said the book on whether it comes back is already written and he doesn’t get to read the last chapter for five years. In this episode: - The 24 hours between finding it himself and hearing the number - Why telling his parents was harder than hearing the diagnosis - What three weeks of not knowing does to someone who built his life on competence - Jewelers Row, twenty cents on the dollar, and the moment Alloy became obvious - The customer who asked to speak to the founder and had them both crying on the phone - Learning to control the controllable, and the chapter he doesn’t get to read for five years - The letter from a friend of eighteen years, and what he’d tell himself on the worst night Subscribe to Through the Valley on YouTube, Spotify, and Apple Podcasts. Brandon’s company, The Alloy Market, sends a free evaluation kit to anyone looking to sell gold. Why There's Shame in Getting Sober but None in the Damage | With The Maze Founder Justin Gurland
Justin Gurland arrived at rehab at eleven at night, three thousand miles from everyone he knew. He woke up the next morning in Los Angeles on Super Bowl Sunday, 2008, gave himself the finger in the mirror, and watched the Giants beat the undefeated Patriots. Then the staff turned off the game, walked everyone into a group room, and asked what each of them believed in. He was twenty-five. He had no community, no sober person anywhere in his life to point at, and no idea what the question meant. What he said was that the Giants had just won and he could hold on to that for now. He describes the moment as meaningless on its face, a football game, a team he wasn't on. It was also the only thing he had. Mark Phillips sits with Justin eighteen years later, five blocks from The Maze, the members club he opened in the Flatiron where hundreds of New Yorkers pay to belong to a building with no alcohol in it. They talk about the sister who told him she couldn't take it anymore, the letter his father hand-wrote for this episode, the Grateful Dead lyric he keeps returning to, and the question he still can't answer: why the shame attaches to getting sober instead of to the damage. In this episode: • Why he says his sister saved his life, and what happens to people who never get that conversation • The Godfather scene he read a month before everything came apart, and why it stayed with him • What he actually said when a counselor asked the room about God • Playing a kids' board game in treatment and feeling his side hurt from laughing for the first time in years • What his father wrote about Justin's lowest moment, and where his relationship with him sits now • Why there is shame in getting sober and none in the harm that came before it • The alcohol-free movement he did not know existed until it was growing in front of him • What he would say if he could sit with himself on the worst night: take this in, and get to work Subscribe to Through the Valley on YouTube, Spotify, and Apple Podcasts. You can find The Maze at themazenyc.com, on Instagram at @themazenyc, and on LinkedIn. Why Brutal Honesty Is the Kindest Thing an Investor Can Do, with VC Coach Charlie O’Donnell
For 20 years, Charlie O'Donnell was the most findable investor in New York. Email on the front page of his site, pitch me anything, come to the dinner. Then in May 2023 he wrote a sentence announcing his last venture deal and stopped. The market didn't push him out. Most people in venture keep raising because it's a good job and there's always a next fund. Charlie ran Brooklyn Bridge Ventures as a solo first-check investor across more than 100 companies, and when he looked at the two available ways to keep doing it into his 40s (hire a younger version of himself, or stop looking at anything pre-revenue) he decided he'd rather not do the job at all than do it that way. Mark Phillips sits with Charlie on what it costs to hold a career loosely: the ice cream shop that went to zero and the conversation he never had with those founders, the marathon he ran badly and blamed on the wind, the 80 days in the NICU where three term sheets got signed, and the firefighter father who played tennis in the morning and did tax returns in the afternoon and was content. In this episode: • Why Charlie stopped raising funds while the option to continue was still open • The tradeoff he now tells every founder about before they take a check • How to hold "good investor" as a job rather than an identity • What 16 collapsed triathletes reveal about experienced high performers • The rounded-up revenue number that quietly ends a fundraise • What his father's illness taught him about asking what a person actually needs • The one thing he realized far too late about being a partner at home Subscribe to Through the Valley on YouTube, Spotify, and Apple Podcasts. Charlie's book, Founder Unfriendly: What Investors Won't Tell You About Getting Funded, is available wherever you buy books, and his newsletter has been running at thisisgoingtobebig.com since 2004.

From Losing Everything at 30 to Building the Firm That Coaches Fortune 100 Executives: Jason Jaggard
Jason Jaggard is the founder of Novus Global, one of the biggest executive coaching firms in the world whose coaches work with Global Executives, professional athletes, and Grammy-winning artists. But at 30, his life collapsed. In a single year, he quit a great job, lost 90% of his revenue, and watched his most important relationship fall apart. We talk about what broke, why it broke, and how that year became the foundation for the firm he leads today. In this first episode of Through the Valley, Jason talks with Mark Phillips about the night he collapsed on his apartment floor, the "cold war" he entered with God, and how the tools he found in his darkest season became the foundation of a coaching firm that now serves some of the most influential leaders on Earth. They cover why blame keeps you stuck, why self-pity is a drug, the difference between psychological safety and psychological strength, and why community is the closest thing to a bulletproof vest a founder can wear. Through the Valley is hosted by Mark Phillips, founder of 11 Tribes Ventures, and explores the seasons of loss, failure, and doubt behind remarkable careers. Deal Highlights - NQS (National Quality Systems)
Founded by multi-time entrepreneur Mark Feinberg, NQS is a vertical AI platform designed to streamline trauma registry management for hospital emergency departments. The company addresses a highly specialized domestic market of approximately 2,400 trauma registry departments—a space previously served by a single, broad-based incumbent whose undifferentiated software left users deeply underserved.
11 Tribes co-invested alongside lead investor Long Run Capital, committing an initial $750,000 check into a priced seed round at an $8 million post-money valuation, with the total raise of $2 million split between the two firms. A defining feature of the investment was NQS's 16 signed hospital contracts at the time of closing—despite the product being six to eight weeks from launch—a rare validation of both market urgency and founder credibility.
Operating partner Carolyn Wilson, former COO of the University of Chicago Health System, provided critical domain expertise during diligence. The round closed in March 2025, the product launched within weeks, and NQS has since grown rapidly. 11 Tribes has made two additional investment tranches, including a recent $750,000 follow-on that effectively constitutes a Series A.

For 20 years, Charlie O'Donnell was the most findable investor in New York. Email on the front page of his site, pitch me anything, come to the dinner. Then in May 2023 he wrote a sentence announcing his last venture deal and stopped.
The market didn't push him out. Most people in venture keep raising because it's a good job and there's always a next fund. • The tradeoff he now tells every founder about before they take a check

• What 16 collapsed triathletes reveal about experienced high performers

• What his father's illness taught him about asking what a person actually needs

From Losing Everything at 30 to Building the Firm That Coaches Fortune 100 Executives: Jason Jaggard
Jason Jaggard is the founder of Novus Global, one of the biggest executive coaching firms in the world whose coaches work with Global Executives, professional athletes, and Grammy-winning artists. But at 30, his life collapsed. In a single year, he quit a great job, lost 90% of his revenue, and watched his most important relationship fall apart. We talk about what broke, why it broke, and how that year became the foundation for the firm he leads today.
In this first episode of Through the Valley, Jason talks with Mark Phillips about the night he collapsed on his apartment floor, the "cold war" he entered with God, and how the tools he found in his darkest season became the foundation of a coaching firm that now serves some of the most influential leaders on Earth.
They cover why blame keeps you stuck, why self-pity is a drug, the difference between psychological safety and psychological strength, and why community is the closest thing to a bulletproof vest a founder can wear.
Through the Valley is hosted by Mark Phillips, founder of 11 Tribes Ventures, and explores the seasons of loss, failure, and doubt behind remarkable careers.

Rebuilt From Nothing & Gave His Life to Other Founders | Michael Dermer @ Lonely Entrepreneur
In October 2008, Michael Dermer had just closed a private equity round at a valuation that validated a decade of work. He had close to 900 employees and a solution wired deep into the Fortune 1000. Within a month, two of his three largest clients ceased to exist and the third needed a government bailout. What followed was three years of twenty-hour days with no defined endpoint, no visible math, and no one to tell him when it would be over. A year earlier he had turned down an offer for the company at a number he still refuses to say out loud. Learning to stop thinking about that number was, in his words, the part of him that had to die. Michael eventually got the company to the other side and sold it. Then a friend said one sentence in a coffee shop that redirected the rest of his life, and The Lonely Entrepreneur was born. In this episode: • What the first thirty days after a black swan event actually feel like from the CEO's chair • The two rules he gave his team when the plan stopped working • Why he insists he never felt lonely, even while building a company named for loneliness • The letter his business partner wrote about him, read aloud for the first time • How he now tells founders to find markets that are worth zero today • Why he believes AI is a 2008-scale reset and what skills survive it • What he would say to himself on the worst night in the valley Subscribe to Through the Valley wherever you listen. New episodes on YouTube, Spotify, and Apple Podcasts. Find Michael at lonelyentrepreneur.com. At 28, Jordan Fliegel had a career-ending injury behind him, thirty employees in front of him, and a startup he loved so much he lived across the street from the office so he could be the first one in. Then his board told him they were replacing him as CEO, and offered him three to five million dollars at a higher valuation if he'd stay quietly and help pick his own replacement. He said yes. Not because he agreed with it, but because saying no meant firing the people he called family. He's never talked about it publicly until now. Jordan is the founder of CoachUp, former co-CEO of DRAFT, and now the founder and CEO of Acquisition Lab, where he helps people buy small businesses instead of starting them. In this conversation with Mark Phillips he walks through the whole valley: the demotion, the year he spent as a president whose title meant nothing, the nine months he slept in a Manhattan office while his next company was insolvent, and the day he finally came back and removed the investors who removed him. In the fall of 2022 Brandon Aversano was 30 years old, away on a trip in California, and found it himself in the middle of the night. Thirty minutes after an ultrasound the chief of urology walked into the room and told him there was a 99% chance it was testicular cancer. His first thought wasn’t about himself. It was how he was going to tell his mom. Nothing could be known before surgery. Three weeks of sitting with whether it was in one spot or everywhere. His dad had prostate cancer the year before. Brandon had built an identity on competence, distinguished scholar, Deloitte, JetBlue, JP Morgan, and the one thing he suddenly couldn’t do was be the capable one. He went on disability the day after scheduling surgery and had free time for the first time in a decade. Mark Phillips sits with Brandon on what that season cost and what it built: the medical debt that horrified a father who hated debt, the trip to Jewelers Row with his grandmother’s jewelry where strangers offered twenty cents on the dollar, the 401k he emptied into a company, the $40,000 mobile app his co-founder told him to scrap, and the surgeon who said the book on whether it comes back is already written and he doesn’t get to read the last chapter for five years. Why There's Shame in Getting Sober but None in the Damage | With The Maze Founder Justin Gurland
Justin Gurland arrived at rehab at eleven at night, three thousand miles from everyone he knew. He woke up the next morning in Los Angeles on Super Bowl Sunday, 2008, gave himself the finger in the mirror, and watched the Giants beat the undefeated Patriots. Then the staff turned off the game, walked everyone into a group room, and asked what each of them believed in. He was twenty-five. He had no community, no sober person anywhere in his life to point at, and no idea what the question meant. What he said was that the Giants had just won and he could hold on to that for now. He describes the moment as meaningless on its face, a football game, a team he wasn't on. It was also the only thing he had. Mark Phillips sits with Justin eighteen years later, five blocks from The Maze, the members club he opened in the Flatiron where hundreds of New Yorkers pay to belong to a building with no alcohol in it. A Threat to Who We Are
Mark Phillips
Apr 20, 2026
19
6
Share
“Meaningless! Meaningless! says the Teacher. Utterly meaningless. Everything is meaningless. What do people gain from all their labors at which they toil under the sun?”
In the 10th century BC, a king of incredible wisdom reigned over one of the greatest civilizations of his time. This man, known as King Solomon, wrestled with challenging questions about the meaning of life. In a book known as Ecclesiastes, he did the difficult work of excavating from his life all that he felt made him important – his wisdom, wealth, and vast kingdom – the things that in his mind made him matter. And when he got down to the bedrock, he realized it had all been a vapor – chasing after the wind.
For many of us, this same feeling of meaninglessness is growing each day as we wrestle with existential questions stemming from the rapid evolution of AI. If you’ve built your sense of meaning on the knowledge work you produce, the answers you provide, and the achievements you’re recognized for, you might be asking, “What is the point of all the work I have done and still prepare to do? If something can think, reason, and create better than I can, where does that leave me?”
Because it threatens the meaning we take from our work, AI threatens what we thought it meant to be human.
And that’s exactly what we need.
The stories in Ecclesiastes show us that even a king with limitless resources and wisdom beyond measure still wrestled with nagging questions of purpose and identity. At the end of his search for meaning–why we work and why we live–Solomon made two observations:
Life is a gift to be received, not a game to be won.
Death finds us all.
For the builders, high-achievers, and go-getters, his first observation lands like a ton of bricks. Isn’t everything a competition? If there’s no scoreboard at the end, is this even a game I want to play? What Solomon discovered is that the foundational source of meaninglessness is our own misguided ambitions. Build something great? Good luck passing it on to someone who will care for it like you have. Cultivate a great reputation? No one is going to remember you in 100 years. It’s chasing after the wind.
While the external world tells us that meaning and permanence is just on the other side of landing one more client, closing one more deal, getting one more win, our internal world–that still, small voice in the back of our minds–is trying to remind us that the pursuit of permanence and meaning through the work of our own hands is, in itself, a form of deeply misguided ambition.
Part of being human is realizing we do not know what will happen. But part of the threat we face is that artificial intelligence was built, designed, and trained to know. Ask it a question about the meaning of life, it will have an answer. Ask it a question about your romantic relationships, it will provide a perspective. Ask it anything, and you’ll receive something in return.
AI was built to know. Humans were designed to ask and to wonder. Our cognitive limitations are not a weakness or flaw, but rather a portal into the part of ourselves that truly makes us human.
There is one universal human experience that AI will never have an answer for: death.
Solomon knew it. And now it is our turn to consider what it might mean for our lives. This technology will reshape how we experience the world around us. But there is so much for us to learn about our inner world through the inevitability of death and the power of the unknown.
The birth of my oldest son, Jackson, was a deeply difficult process–one that left my wife bedridden in sheer exhaustion and landed Jackson in the NICU. There were moments during the delivery where I did not know if Emily was going to make it. When a team of seven doctors and nurses descend on your hospital room, your mind goes to some scary places. There is such a fine line between life and death in those moments. And all the while, I stood there helplessly, providing the occasional ice-chip and word of encouragement, but at a total loss to help, support, or save the person I love most deeply in this world.
Confronting, for even just a moment, the reality of death for my wife, quickly dismantled the weak scaffolding I had used to prop up my own identity–an identity built on control, usefulness, and achievement. For the first time, the reality that I was not enough and the outcome was not in my control finally took root.
But there was a moment after all of the chaos had subsided, Emily was sleeping upstairs and I was down in the NICU with Jackson. My sister, a nurse practitioner by training, was with me and Jackson was hooked up to what seemed like a thousand different wires. My sister, knowing that I was a deer in the headlights, jumped into action, moving a chair across the room, tugging on the wires to create some slack, and placing Jackson on my chest. I’ll never forget that moment. It may have been the first moment in my life that I was truly present–not feigning presence to accomplish a goal or meet my ambitions–no longer working to control the outcome.
Just present.
Deeply emotionally attuned.
And beginning a journey of identity reformation that is still happening today.
This is the power of not knowing. And this is the power of death. Death in the physical form, yes, but also death of the false narratives that we think bring us life. For me that was control, enough-ness, success in all things. All of those were shattered to pieces in one day at Central DuPage Hospital, and yet incredible beauty followed as I was able to hold and experience life with my son. I believe I am a better father–a better human being–because I have accepted that one day I will die. And I know the same fate will find those I love the most.
As we grapple with what AI means for our world and for ourselves, I have to believe that this uniquely human experience can and should inform how we see our place in the world.
We face something that threatens what we thought it meant to be human. But if a machine can do it, maybe it was never as important as we thought.
When we rest in our limitations, we can finally stop performing. We can stop measuring our worth by how fast we think or how much we produce or how many answers we can have. We can release the pressure to be the smartest person in the room, because the smartest person in the room is no longer a person.
What remains is everything a machine cannot do. Suffer and yet persist. Love someone you might lose. Choose to move forward in the face of fear. These are not the leftovers of the human experience. They are what make us who we are.
The person who has come face to face with their own limitations and the reality of death is the person who understands what it truly means to be human–they are the person who will never be replaced by AI. Not because the information they have collected is rare, but because the formation they have experienced is real.

A letter to my co-founder that nobody knows.
A thank-you to the one who carried the weight no one else could see.
Mark Phillips
Sep 02, 2026
10
1
Share
Thank you for understanding that leadership is hard. Thank you for acknowledging that it can be lonely without making me feel like I’m doing something wrong.
Thank you for how patiently you sit and listen and absorb the wild swings of my day. I know that most of what I share with you is the bad news – the things that have recently found their way under my skin.
But I never tell you how beautiful this crazy thing we’re doing together is to me. I never tell you about the success because it never feels like enough.
I wonder why that is.
And as I share all the bad news, thank you for valiantly holding the present challenges with the reality of “if this fails, what will we do then?”
And thank you for not panicking when it all feels like it’s falling apart because I’m looking to you for stability more than you know.
Thank you for being steady especially in the moments when I am pretending to be.
Thank you for being the rich soil of my own growth. All I have ever wanted as a leader is to grow, but I see now that the seeds of growth in my own life would have withered and died apart from the rich soil of your belief in me.
So, thank you for being my co-founder that nobody knows. And for better or worse, till death do us part, I am so glad I also get to call you my wife.

2023 was a year of incredible growth at 11 Tribes Ventures. As our team has engaged in year-end reflection and 2024 planning, multifaceted, intentional growth was a consistent theme. We experienced growth within our team, growth at the AUM level, and growth of reputation within the market, culminating in over two-thousand companies approaching us for investment.
This culminates in what I believe will be a robust and banner year for 11 Tribes. But, as with any yearly review, I would be remiss if I did not comment on how far we have come.
We launched our firm during a global pandemic, watched as investor behavior became undisciplined amidst a zero-interest rate environment, and stood by as the Federal Reserve raised rates more aggressively than ever before - leading to the literal collapse of two banks.
Many of the news articles you read will tell you that it was one of the most difficult environments for venture capital; while this may be true with fundraising levels at historic lows, this past year only helped to validate our thesis.
Despite the headwinds, we expanded our team, launched 11 Tribes Ventures Fund II, and raised over $20M. But more importantly, we heard from countless entrepreneurs that our strategy – rejecting a growth at all costs mentality in favor of sustainable, durable, and profitable growth – is deeply needed.
The Greek philosopher Heraclitus once postulated that “There is nothing permanent except change.”
Venture capital is changing.
And it is in this change that 11 Tribes has found its purpose.
Below is the best collection of data we saw on venture in 2023 as well as the eight most salient lessons learned from this past year. We hope you enjoy.
The best chart I saw in 2023:
Believe it or not, this chart tells you everything you need to know about investing in the venture capital asset class.
The venture capital asset class has generated greater returns than any other asset class over the last 15 years. But,
Venture capital also has the largest dispersion between top decile and median performance.
What does that all mean? Venture has been one of the most significant wealth creation vehicles of the last three decades, but largely due to access and investment minimums, these returns have been restricted to pension funds and endowments.
But as emerging funds like 11 Tribes have begun to compete, participating not as financiers, but as operationally minded, value-additive partners to entrepreneurs, the strategy of remaining small and agile as a fund has become a competitive advantage (more data on this below).
In summary – find the right manager, with the right GP-thesis fit, and the opportunity to generate returns will be significant.
Lessons Learned in 2023:
The focus on the founder outcome is the bedrock of our thesis and core to every investment. This past year brought more clarity and conviction in our need to optimize for both founder and business outcomes, ensuring that financial returns are not generated at the expense of the founder’s wellbeing.
With this comes its own set of challenges. When we acknowledge the human at the helm, our feedback can be perceived as an endorsement or an indictment of the business. Entrepreneurs, for the first time in a long time, feel seen and understood when we share our unique thesis. We welcome this, but also recognize that it requires we handle each interaction with intentionality and grace, ensuring that our acknowledgement of the human is not misunderstood as endorsement of the business.
Our robust LP-base is steadily becoming a competitive differentiator and value-add to our entire portfolio. From day one, we prioritized providing access to this dynamic asset class and somewhat inadvertently, built a broad set of investors, many of whom come from entrepreneurial backgrounds. With the addition of our newest partner and head of platform, Jeff Baxter, we are turning this dynamic network into a weapon for growth.
We invite you to unpack the entirety of the data for yourself here, but in summary, an analysis of 2,500 funds from 1980-2023 revealed that small funds ($5-50M) had:
The highest average return of 2.3x (compared to 2.1x for funds between $50-200M, 1.8x for funds between $200-500M, and 1.6x for funds between $500M-$1B+)
The highest probability of “outperforming” (5x or higher). The data revealed that funds sized $0-50M are 1.4x, 3.0x and 12.0x more likely to generate a 5x+ outcome than funds sized $50-200M, $200-500M and $500M-$1B respectively.
Lastly, the relative distribution of outperforming funds showed that there are almost as many 5x+ funds sized $0-50M as they are in any other fund size category combined.
No one truly knows where the market is headed. We choose to remain disciplined, patient, and opportunistic.
The hype of 2020-2022 was exceptionally damaging to the venture ecosystem, and furthermore, undisciplined investing with outrageous valuations do not predict a strong future outcome or future fundraising success. We have avoided and continue to avoid these inflated rounds.
Prioritizing the jockey (of the horse and jockey analogy) has never been more important. We would prefer an A-team with a B-idea over an A-idea with a B-team every time.
Brand matters in VC. Our brand has become known, well regarded, and deeply appreciated. Consequences of this brand affinity and recognition has been stronger deal-flow, enhanced investor relationships, and more opportunities to provide support and add value to our portfolio of companies.

A Failed Startup, An Identity Crisis, and a VC Company That Cares with Mark Phillips
Feb 3
Written By Clay Stelzer
Most venture capitalists will pitch you on their portfolio companies, their returns, their network.
Mark Phillips will ask you about your mental health.
In this week's episode of Fearful Giants, I sat down with Mark Phillips, Managing Partner of 11 Tribes Ventures - a VC firm doing something most investors won't touch: putting founder resilience at the center of their investment thesis.
Mark and I met through friends in the VC community, and what struck me immediately was his honesty about failure. Not the glossy "I failed fast and pivoted" story you hear at conferences. The real kind. The kind that breaks you open.
Before founding 11 Tribes, Mark built a medical device company for type 1 diabetics while in business school. It was going to be huge. Forbes cover, the whole dream. Except it wasn't. The company failed. He couldn't raise the capital. He got leapfrogged by competitors.
And when he finally stopped long enough to look around at his life, he realized: his marriage was struggling, his health was shot, his faith felt distant. Everything that actually mattered was in shambles.
That identity crisis became the foundation for 11 Tribes Ventures, where the tagline is "capital and care" and the thesis is simple: founder outcomes matter as much as business outcomes.
“Your worth is not your company.”
— Mark Phillips
In This Episode, We Talk About:
How Mark's startup failure led to a complete identity crisis
Why 70% of VCs laugh when he talks about founder wellbeing
The hidden cost of believing your worth comes from your business
How meditation literally changed the way Mark's brain works
What it looks like when a founder kills a major partnership to protect what matters
The truth that grounds Mark when fear tries to take over
My Key Takeaways from this conversation with Mark:
1. Your worth is not your company. If Mark could whisper one truth into every leader's ear, it would be this. He wishes someone had told him 12 years ago. It would have saved him years of pain. Too many founders tie their entire identity to their business - and when that business struggles or fails, they collapse with it.
2. Most of the market is scared of this conversation. When Mark pitches his model, 70% of people respond with disdain or condescension. At an event last night, a guy literally laughed at him. These people are scared because their entire identity is wrapped up in how hard they work. The other 30%? When he finds them, it's magic. They get it. They've been through something. They have what one of Mark's investors calls "a limp."
3. Founder resilience isn't a nice-to-have - it's a competitive advantage. 11 Tribes invests in companies where they believe founder wellbeing will directly correlate with better business outcomes. Not weaker founders who work less. Stronger founders who can sustain the long game. They're trying to prove that by investing in the founder outcome - mental, emotional, physical, spiritual health - they can actually create more sustainable and profitable businesses.
4. Slowing down is not optional if you want to lead well. Mark's closing words hit hard: "The crisis we have as leaders is that we are busy and we are in hurry." He wasn't fun to be around when he was grinding. He was so focused on his goals that he didn't have time to care about people. Now? Meditation is non-negotiable. He processes the world differently. He honors his emotions differently. He feels cognitively different when he skips it.
5. Being loved is what allows you to move forward through fear. When I asked Mark what truth helps him rise when fear drags him down, he said: "That I am loved." For him, it starts with his relationship with Jesus, then filters down to his wife and kids. Life is scary. Leadership is scary. But resting in that love - in those connections that actually matter - allows him to keep moving forward.This conversation with Julie left me thinking about how much fear many leaders carry around being seen, being wrong, or not being "enough." And how much of leadership - whether you're running a company, advising families, or just showing up in your own life - is about doing it anyway.
This conversation with Mark reminded me that the best leaders aren't the ones who can endure the most pain. They're the ones brave enough to stop, to reassess, and to build something that doesn't require them to burn out to succeed.
Are you part of the 70% who would laugh at the idea that founder wellbeing matters? Listen anyway. You might be surprised.

The Wisdom Economy
In a world where everything is known, what truly matters is how we live.
Mark Phillips
Oct 23, 2025
7
2
1
Share
By now, you’ve experienced some level of change in your personal and professional life because of Artificial Intelligence. Personally, it has made me significantly more productive, and it has made a material difference in our team’s ability to remain small while engaging in a level of diligence previously unattainable for a team our size.
But productivity is merely a byproduct of a much larger shift that AI is creating. In his article, Knowledge Work is Dying - Here’s What Comes Next, Joe Hudson makes a powerful observation.
AI models don’t sleep or burn out; they can absorb entire fields of study in days. One highly trained model will soon be able to outperform an expert in physics, law, and engineering – simultaneously at any hour. Facts, skills, and expertise will be increasingly commoditized, and even the smartest of us will be replaceable.
It’s easy to overlook how radical that is. Our entire society is built around knowledge as a scarce, precious resource. School systems, standardized tests, college pipelines, job interviews, LinkedIn profiles are all mechanisms to measure, prove, and reward how much you know… Now, imagine a world where all that is irrelevant, akin to the ability to build a fire today—occasionally useful, but mostly unnecessary in a world with light bulbs, central heating, and stove tops.
Enter the Wisdom Economy.
When knowledge is no longer scarce, what remains valuable? Wisdom. You can get answers about anything from AI, but how you use those answers takes wisdom.
Wisdom is how to live. It is the residue of mistakes, metabolized by time and reflection. It cannot be rushed, and it cannot be coded. It is an embodied – as in felt in the body – experience, guidance from the inside.
As someone who turns to Biblical truth for guidance in all things, the book of James tells us that “Wisdom from above is first pure, then peaceable, gentle, open to reason, full of mercy and good fruits, impartial and sincere.”
A powerful mindset to strive for.
This shift is on par with the industrial revolution which moved us from labor to leverage and the information revolution which moved society from leverage to knowledge.
As we meet and analyze thousands of businesses each year, we are seeing a distinct shift away from the power of knowledge and acknowledging that (as Isaac on our team recently noted) the winners will be those who recognize that competitive moats are not about data or knowledge, they’re about creating systems that generate, process, and learn from data better than anyone else.
The frontier has moved. Knowledge is abundant; wisdom is scarce.
As we enter this next era, may we be the kind of builders and investors who don’t just ask what’s possible, but what’s wise.
That will be the real competitive advantage for our companies, our teams, and our lives.

Attention Follows Action
“We all wear masks, and the time comes when we cannot remove them without removing some of our own skin.” – André Berthiaume
Mark Phillips
Mar 04, 2025
4
Share
There is nothing more terrifying than having your deepest self truly seen.
But what makes it even harder? Knowing that others are watching.
One of my favorite things to do is talk business ideas with friends - not just because I love new ideas, but because they reveal something deeper. Every idea is a glimpse into someone’s worldview - their frustrations, their aspirations, and, most of all, their willingness to be seen. It's a chance for me to pay attention.
I have one friend in particular whose imagination is running wild right now. Ideas are tumbling out, experiments are being run, and insight is growing. But as we tried to find time to discuss his latest idea, he shared a hard truth:
“I’m hesitating because I feel like my plan is not very impressive and maybe kind of sucks.”
Sound familiar?
How about this translation?
"I'm hesitating because I feel like I don't know what I'm doing and I question my ability to make this thing work."
We’ve all been there - the fear that if we put our ideas out into the world, the attention of others will expose our own shortcomings.
His words hit home. I remembered that exact feeling when I first shared the idea for 11 Tribes. The emotions were a mixture of embarrassment, awkwardness, and fear. Business has this remarkable knack of manifesting the values and passion we feel internally, turning them into outward signals of our soul.
There really is nothing more terrifying than having your deepest self truly seen.
But there is nothing more rewarding than facing that fear and choosing to move forward.
And here is the paradox - the moment you do, people will notice. And that might be the scariest part. Their attention can feel like a weight - but it can also be proof that you’re doing something worth noticing.
Fear doesn’t disappear before action - it disappears because of action.
So move forward. Take ground. Action is the antidote to fear.
One of my favorite authors is Erwin McManus. He lived a childhood gripped with fear but through faith, he has found true freedom. His words below are a continuous reminder of the arbitrary constraints we place on ourselves.
“If you’re afraid of heights, you stay low. If you’re afraid of people, you stay alone. If you’re afraid of the dark, you stay in the light. Your fear establishes the boundaries of your freedom.”
Keep working on the Inner Game

What Does It Cost to Look Good?
A Reflection on Leadership, Ego, and Care
Mark Phillips
Jan 14, 2026
6
1
Share
”Humility is not thinking less of yourself, it’s thinking of yourself less.” — C.S. Lewis
My elementary school was small. Sixteen kids in the eighth-grade class. The classrooms were built onto the back of an old church, and the building surrounded a blacktop parking lot that transformed into the ultimate athletic proving ground during recess. Basketball, football, four square, freeze tag—you name a recess favorite, we had a ranking from first all the way to last.
The competition was fierce. And it demanded a price, which we paid gladly: scuffed shoes, tattered pants, and that thawing hand ache after an epic game of basketball in mid-December. Those are cherished memories for me, not because of any performance or ranking, but because those moments on the blacktop were the first time I can remember feeling like a leader.
“The other kids look to Mark to put together the teams at recess.”
“If I ever need help getting the students in line, I know I can ask Mark, and he’ll get it done.”
“He is the leader of our class. And his loud voice really helps.”
That last one feels like a blessing and a curse, but we all have our own unique gifts, right?
Those teachers saw in me what I felt in myself, a natural inclination to lead. But on the blacktop of Faith Christian Elementary, leadership meant I got to pick the captains, set the rules, and—if I was feeling generous—make sure my team got the ball first. It gave me control, a reputation that felt good, and a place to use that loud voice, everything that, as the youngest of four, I craved.
That blacktop didn’t require much reflection. Leadership felt effortless, control without cost, validation without sacrifice. It took years, and much higher stakes, for me to learn that leadership is a heavy responsibility. One that challenges a leader’s ego and forces them into impossible decisions, moments when protecting your image and seeking external validation are in direct opposition with doing what’s right.
These childhood moments taught me that control felt good because it made me look good—capable, worthy of being followed. What it didn’t teach me is that real leadership requires relinquishing control over how you’re perceived, surrendering the need to always look right, in order to serve that which you have been entrusted to steward.
***
This tension between protecting how we’re seen and doing what’s needed shows up everywhere. In boardrooms and family rooms. In pitch meetings and parent-teacher conferences. But I’ve rarely seen it articulated as honestly as it was in a recent post on Reddit.
The website describes itself as the front page of the internet, and as we know, the internet can be a strange place. Interested in heavyweight boxing, cleaning products, or cats doing tricks? Reddit has a page for you. But what makes it particularly interesting is the nature of its content. Because users can post anonymously, it’s become a repository of honest, vulnerable, and deeply compelling human experience.
On a recent visit to the “Entrepreneur” page, I was struck by the raw truth of one user’s post:
Everyone talks about the risk of entrepreneurship. The sleepless nights. The grind that never stops. But no one talks about:
The awkward feeling of telling friends and family about your business and seeing zero excitement.
The crippling anxiety of seeing someone else launch your exact same idea, but with a bigger budget and better connections.
The way your confidence gets ripped apart when a random stranger calls your product ‘meh’.
The identity crisis when you realize your whole personality has become work.
Sobering. But what was left unsaid is as telling as what the original poster shared.
He didn’t mention setting vision and strategy, defining customer value, driving growth, or hiring leaders. None of the tactical work of launching a company. What he had come to realize, like many leaders before him, is that the tactical challenges pale in comparison to what leadership demands of our ego.
Healthy leadership comes with a price that is much steeper than scuffed shoes and tattered pants. It demands the slow, internal work of relinquishing ego. Relinquishing the parts of ourselves that crave what the world cannot reliably give: validation, consistently “looking good”, and the comfort of always being seen as right. This kind of surrender is not a one-time event. It comes in waves, often in the moments that matter most.
But this isn’t just an entrepreneurial problem. Parenting a toddler. Teaching a classroom. Managing a family budget. Caring for an aging parent. At some point, each of us will step into a leadership role and reckon with this same tension.
The whole process hurts. Making decisions that serve the outcome rather than your image is excruciating. You will look bad. People will question your judgment. You will begin to doubt yourself. But when that moment finds us, we must choose: will we make the decision that protects our ego, or the one that serves what we are stewarding?
This is the shift from control to care. And when we make it, everything changes:
We stop optimizing for being right and start taking responsibility for what actually works.
Control keeps us tense and reactive, managing every outcome, while care invites humility—the freedom to admit we don’t have all the answers.
Control demands a constant stream of achievement, while care keeps us grounded, attentive, and emotionally available.
A shift from control to care moves us from ego-protection to durable growth.
My executive coach, Jon, loves to say that grace is a gift, but growth is a choice. And he is absolutely right. When we care about the outcome as opposed to controlling for our image, we make choices that are fraught with risk, sure to involve pain, and almost guaranteed to make us look bad. And yet this is the only path to healthy leadership.
Again, this is not a one-time decision. Once we care for the outcome rather than our ego, the work isn’t magically done. In fact, the hardest work is just beginning. It comes in waves, in ordinary moments, across every domain of life:
A parent who commits to a consistent bedtime routine instead of ‘just getting it done’ quickly learns that care requires patience, repetition, and discipline even when the tantrums make them feel like they’re failing.
A coach who benches their most talented player to protect team culture doesn’t get relief—they get questions about their judgment and whispers that they don’t know how to win.
A teacher who holds the line on expectations discovers that care means explaining the same standard again and again, absorbing student frustration and parent complaints, even when lowering the bar would make everyone like them more.
Care trades the pressure and illusion of control for the discipline of presence. It replaces quick wins with sustained responsibility.
***
At 11 Tribes, we have established ourselves as the firm where capital and care converge. I haven’t read every venture firm’s vision statement, but it’s uncommon to hear care used as a defining posture in venture investing. And yet, if more venture investors reflected on what it could mean to move from control to care, I suspect the idea would feel surprisingly compelling.
Most venture investors, whether they realize it or not, make decisions to protect their own ego. They soften feedback to preserve relationships. They delay hard conversations to avoid being seen as the bad guy. They protect founders’ egos because doing so protects their own.
But when investors protect egos (both theirs and founders’), everyone loses. Founders don’t get the truth they need. Companies don’t get the course corrections that could save them. And investors end up complicit in outcomes they saw coming but didn’t have the courage to name. Outcomes that needed care but only received reputational control.
At 11 Tribes, we’ve made a different choice. We have found that when we relinquish control over how we are perceived—surrendering our ego to care for the outcomes we have committed to serve—remarkable things happen:
Care gives us permission to tell the truth early
In a control environment, feedback is often delayed or softened to preserve access, influence, or reputation. Care does the opposite. Because 11 Tribes is committed to the long-term health of the founder and the company, we name issues early and directly. Care does not avoid hard conversations—it demands them.
Care allows us to challenge without threatening identity
Founders do not resist feedback because they dislike improvement. They resist it because it feels like an attack on who they are. When relationships are built with care, we can separate performance from identity. That distinction creates the psychological safety required for honest dialogue about leadership gaps, blind spots, or necessary change.
Care enables accountability without ego protection
Because we are not trying to control how we are perceived, we can hold our founders accountable to the outcomes they themselves have chosen. Care means we establish commitments, create timelines, assume excellence, and anchor accountability.
***
The blacktop leadership of my childhood cost me nothing. Real leadership costs everything our ego wants to protect. When we choose to care for outcomes rather than control for our own image, we will look bad. We will face criticism. And we will doubt ourselves. I certainly have. But this is what healthy leadership demands.
The founders we serve, the children we raise, the teams we build, the outcomes we steward—they don’t need leaders who always look good. They need leaders willing to do what’s right, even when it’s costly.
This is the shift from control to care. And it’s the only choice that allows us to bear the full weight of what we’ve been entrusted to lead.

What My Mom Knew
Mark Phillips
May 21, 2026
21
1
Share
I want to talk about it.
I keep anchoring to that truth as I deal with the sadness and grief of losing my Mom.
She died on May 1st. I have never grieved something of this magnitude, and it’s easy to worry that I am grieving in the “wrong way.”
But what I know is true, and what I know is right, is that I want to talk about it. Talking helps me process my emotions. But more importantly, talking about my Mom honors her legacy and it helps me remember. To that end, below is what I shared about my Mom at her Celebration of Life.
Ask me about it.
Tell me how it made you feel.
Tell me what you learned about my Mom from these words.
Ask me anything, because I want to talk about it and I want to remember my Mom.
Eleven days before my Mom died from an inoperable hemorrhage on her brain stem, I wrote these words.
This is the power of death. Death in the physical form, yes, but also death of the false narratives that we think bring us life. For me that was control, enough-ness, success in all things. All of those were shattered to pieces in one day at Central DuPage Hospital, and yet incredible beauty followed as I was able to hold and experience life with my son. I believe I am a better father, a better human being, because I have accepted that one day I will die. And I know the same fate will find those I love the most.
What remains is everything a machine cannot do. Suffer and yet persist. Love someone you might lose. Choose to move forward in the face of fear. These are not the leftovers of the human experience. They are what make us who we are. The person who has come face to face with their own limitations and the reality of death is the person who understands what it truly means to be human. They are the person who will never be replaced. Not because the information they collected is rare, but because the formation they have experienced is real.
Reading those words, two weeks removed from the deepest sorrow and grief of my life, is oddly settling. Not because it was prophetic or a fateful prediction, but because it was an acknowledgment that this human experience is broken and death is the culmination of the brokenness. And while the grief of this tragedy brings me to my knees time and time again, I also know that I am not the first, nor will I be the last, to taste the bitterness of this broken world.
For much of my life, I was uncomfortable at funerals. The unease stemmed from not knowing what to say. Put me in front of a grieving parent, child, sibling, or spouse and I felt helpless. What can one say?
Sitting on the other side of that exchange today, I can confidently tell you there is nothing to say. Human nature is to use words to soften the blow, find the silver lining, lessen the pain. But the reality of death is full of pain. And there is only one way through that pain. The way is through. Not around, not under, but through. That is how we honor my Mom. That is how we honor her beautiful life. And that is how we honor our own emotions.
God does not waste anything. Over the last two weeks, I have seen such beauty in my Mom’s passing. Friends weeping with us as we encounter the newest wave of grief. A community rallying around a family in need. Countless opportunities to share what I believe to be the most important part of my Mom’s life. The fact that she is now in heaven, in the presence of her Savior, Jesus Christ. This is the formation that death brings. And I believe it is the most beautiful part of being human.
Growing up, my Mom would often share that “life’s not fair and you should be thankful it’s not”. Goodness that frustrated me as a young man. Whether it was sports, academics, relationships, or anything else high school boys get frustrated about, Mom always stayed firmly rooted in her belief that life’s not fair. Now, don’t misunderstand, certainly there are so many with deeply challenging circumstances, but just to be born and to take a breath today and to feel the sun on your skin is a miracle of magnitudes we cannot compute. But sometimes that knife cuts the other way — it doesn’t feel fair that my Mom’s life was cut short. It doesn’t feel fair that she died four weeks before my wife is due to give birth to our fourth son. It doesn’t feel fair that my Dad has to rebuild his life with a gapping hole at the center that he cannot fill. None of that is fair.
But what my Mom knew was that the greatest injustice was not something that happened to us but what has been done for us.
Jesus of Nazareth, the Son of God, who lived a perfect life, died on the cross to pay the price for my Mom’s life, for my life, and for your life. What my Mom knew deep in her soul was that through His death and resurrection he has given us the opportunity of true freedom in this life and in the next.
So standing before you today, I have hope.
I have hope for the future. I have hope knowing that I will see my Mom again one day. It doesn’t take away the pain - I miss my Mom a lot. But the pain has been redeemed, it has been bought for a price, and it draws me closer to the same Savior that my Mom followed so faithfully for all of her days.

Before we dive into our regularly scheduled programming, I want to make you aware of an upcoming webinar 11 Tribes is hosting. This webinar will cover Fund 1 performance to date, outlook on the market, and the investment opportunity available for Fund 2. We'd be delighted if you'd attend - register here.
What You Need to Know:
Our strategy and thesis is working. Fund 1 performance remains very strong with a 2.7X Multiple on Invested Capital (MOIC) and 62.7% IRR across 33 portfolio companies. We anticipate our first exit from the fund this calendar year.
Fund 2 is accelerating towards a final close in the next six months. We now have capital commitments of $23.5M (goal of $40M). With early stage valuations down ~40% from peak levels, is now the right time to make a commitment?
You need to know about the remarkable tax advantage known as Qualified Small Business Stock (QSBS). It has been called perhaps the most attractive tax exemption in the entire IRS Code. QSBS exemption means that there is zero federal capital gains tax for you as an investor (LP) from the sale of qualifying stock that is held for more than five years. The large majority of our investments will be qualifying stock held for five years. If you'd like to learn more, reach out and let's discuss.
We are excited to announce our inaugural Founder Summit this June in Chicago. We will be hosting ~40 of our founders in partnership with The Table Group. We are actively reviewing sponsorship opportunities for the summit - if you’d like your organization to be involved, let us know.
What do we think about Artificial Intelligence?
Compared to your average venture capital firm, we talk about Artificial Intelligence far less. This is not a result of a lack of interest in the technology itself (we find it fascinating), but rather the undisciplined investing behavior when it comes to the "next big AI company". As an asset class, venture has become a consensus investing club that has created a frenzy of overpriced deals in AI just as we have seen during the dot com era, the advent of SaaS business models, and most recently with blockchain and crypto.
To put it simply, when investing in a pre-revenue, AI company at a $50M valuation, all of the value has been priced out.
That being said, as investors we have to reckon with how the technology will undoubtedly reshape the venture capital asset class, just as it is doing with so many other industries (you can read about a few reasons why here). Sam Altman (Founder of OpenAI) recently said that he believes we are not far from AI enabling the first single person, billion dollar company. A bold (and likely true) proclamation.
But we see a flip side to that prediction. The same technology will also lead to the proliferation of smaller, much more capital efficient businesses that choose to exit on a reasonable timeline for ~$100M. Very few venture capital firms are asking the hard, self-introspective questions on how to fund and generate returns from this next generation of startups.
At 11 Tribes, we've been building for this type of company for several years. We call these enduring companies. Not in the sense that they will last forever, but in the sense that they can endure hardship and emerge on the other side stronger.
So, what do these enduring companies need?
Thoughtful, properly sized capital infusions. The single largest expense for early-stage startups is payroll. With AI doing the work of an entire engineering, sales, or customer success department, these companies will need much less capital. Our goal has always been to stay small so as to meet the needs of our founders (multi-billion dollar funds cannot say the same).
Resilience and organizational health. For anyone who has built a company, you know the joy that comes from working in a small team.
But you also know how hard it can be when there is disharmony and no place to hide. The 11 Tribes Founder Resilience Commitment is a first of its kind allocation of capital that amplifies the amazing potential of our founders and mitigates the risk of a litany of people related issues that can kill companies.
This is a seminal moment in the evolution of venture capital. We would be naïve to suggest that the asset class will look the same in ten years as it does today. There has never been a better time to be part of 11 Tribes and to optimize for both founder and business outcomes.
